name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MOLECULAR_BASIS_OF_INHERITANCE_MCQ_Q01 - Linkage of nucleotides in a DNA strand

questiontext.text: In a DNA strand the nucleotides are linked together by:

generalfeedback.text:
Conceptual Principle
A polynucleotide chain consists of recurring nucleotide subunits joined linearly to form the sugar-phosphate backbone of nucleic acids.

Evaluation of Concepts
Within an individual strand of DNA, adjacent deoxynucleotides are joined when the phosphate group attached to the 5'-carbon of one sugar is esterified to the 3'-hydroxyl group of the adjacent pentose sugar. This covalent linkage forms a repeating 3'-5' phosphodiester bond along the single strand. In contrast, glycosidic bonds connect the nitrogenous base to the pentose sugar at the 1'-carbon, hydrogen bonds hold the two complementary strands together between opposing nitrogenous base pairs, and peptide bonds join amino acids in polypeptide chains.

Final Conclusion
Adjacent nucleotides within a single DNA strand are linked together by phosphodiester bonds.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MOLECULAR_BASIS_OF_INHERITANCE_MCQ_Q02 - Structural difference between nucleoside and nucleotide

questiontext.text: A nucleoside differs from a nucleotide. It lacks the:

generalfeedback.text:
Conceptual Principle
Nucleic acid building blocks consist of nitrogenous bases, pentose sugars, and phosphate groups organized hierarchically as nucleosides and nucleotides.

Evaluation of Concepts
A nucleoside is composed solely of a nitrogenous base attached to the 1'-carbon of a pentose sugar (ribose or deoxyribose) via an N-glycosidic linkage. When a phosphate group is attached to the 5'-hydroxyl group of this nucleoside through a phosphoester bond, the resulting molecule is a nucleotide (a nucleoside monophosphate). Thus, a nucleoside specifically lacks the phosphate moiety present in a nucleotide.

Final Conclusion
A nucleoside differs from a nucleotide because it lacks the phosphate group.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MOLECULAR_BASIS_OF_INHERITANCE_MCQ_Q03 - Sugar classification of deoxyribose and ribose

questiontext.text: Both deoxyribose and ribose belong to a class of sugars called:

generalfeedback.text:
Conceptual Principle
Monosaccharides are classified based on the number of carbon atoms contained in their carbon skeleton.

Evaluation of Concepts
Ribose has the chemical formula \( \text{C}_5\text{H}_{10}\text{O}_5 \) and deoxyribose (specifically 2-deoxy-D-ribose) has the chemical formula \( \text{C}_5\text{H}_{10}\text{O}_4 \). Because each of these monosaccharide molecules contains a backbone composed of five carbon atoms, both belong to the carbohydrate class known as pentoses. Trioses contain three carbon atoms, hexoses contain six carbon atoms, and polysaccharides are high-molecular-weight polymers of monosaccharide units.

Final Conclusion
Both ribose and deoxyribose are five-carbon sugars classified as pentoses.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MOLECULAR_BASIS_OF_INHERITANCE_MCQ_Q04 - Effect of purine and pyrimidine pairing

questiontext.text: The fact that a purine base always pairs through hydrogen bonds with a pyrimidine base in the DNA double helix leads to:

generalfeedback.text:
Conceptual Principle
The geometric architecture of the B-DNA double helix relies on strict complementary base pairing between purines and pyrimidines across the opposing strands.

Evaluation of Concepts
Purines (adenine and guanine) have a bulky, two-ring bicyclic structure, whereas pyrimidines (thymine and cytosine) have a smaller, single-ring monocyclic structure. If two purines paired together, the width of the helix would be noticeably wider, and if two pyrimidines paired together, the helix would be noticeably narrower. Pairing a bulky two-ring purine consistently with a smaller single-ring pyrimidine ensures that the distance between the two sugar-phosphate backbones remains virtually constant at approximately \( 2.0\text{ nm} \) (\( 20\text{ Å} \)) all along the helical molecule.

Final Conclusion
Constant pairing of a purine with a pyrimidine generates a uniform width throughout the DNA double helix.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MOLECULAR_BASIS_OF_INHERITANCE_MCQ_Q05 - Net electric charge on DNA and histones

questiontext.text: The net electric charge on DNA and histones is:

generalfeedback.text:
Conceptual Principle
Eukaryotic DNA packaging into chromatin depends on electrostatic interactions between the nucleic acid polymer and packaging proteins.

Evaluation of Concepts
The phosphate groups that form the backbone of a DNA molecule carry negative charges due to ionised oxygen atoms at physiological pH, rendering DNA overall negatively charged. Histone proteins are basic proteins enriched in basic amino acid residues such as lysine and arginine, whose side chains carry positive charges at physiological pH. These opposing charges allow the negatively charged DNA strand to wrap tightly around the positively charged octameric histone core to assemble nucleosomes.

Final Conclusion
The net electric charge on DNA is negative and on histones is positive.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MOLECULAR_BASIS_OF_INHERITANCE_MCQ_Q06 - Positions of promoter and terminator in transcription

questiontext.text: The promoter site and the terminator site for transcription are located at:

generalfeedback.text:
Conceptual Principle
In molecular biology, positions and orientations in a transcription unit are conventionally defined relative to the coding strand (which runs in the 5' to 3' direction).

Evaluation of Concepts
A transcription unit in DNA contains three essential functional regions: a promoter, the structural gene, and a terminator. With reference to the coding strand, the promoter is situated towards the 5'-end (designated as upstream of the structural gene) where RNA polymerase binds. The terminator is situated towards the 3'-end (designated as downstream of the structural gene) where RNA synthesis terminates.

Final Conclusion
The promoter and terminator are located at the 5' (upstream) end and 3' (downstream) end, respectively, of the transcription unit.

answer.text: 3' (downstream) end and 5' (upstream) end, respectively of the transcription unit
5' (upstream) end and 3' (downstream) end, respectively of the transcription unit

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MOLECULAR_BASIS_OF_INHERITANCE_MCQ_Q07 - Characteristics and manifestations of sickle cell anaemia

questiontext.text: Which of the following statements is the most appropriate for sickle cell anaemia?

generalfeedback.text:
Conceptual Principle
Sickle cell anaemia is an autosomal recessive genetic disorder caused by a qualitative molecular alteration in the haemoglobin polypeptide.

Evaluation of Concepts
A single point mutation in the gene encoding the \( \beta \)-globin chain substitutes valine for glutamic acid at the sixth position. Because this defect is structural and genetic rather than an iron deficiency, iron supplementation cannot correct or treat the disease. As the disease originates from an altered single polypeptide molecule, it represents a classic molecular disease. Additionally, individuals who carry the sickle cell trait (heterozygotes) experience lower mortality from falciparum malaria because erythrocyte sickling disrupts the intracellular life cycle of the malaria parasite.

Final Conclusion
Sickle cell anaemia is an untreatable disease via iron supplements, a molecular genetic disorder, and protective against severe malaria; therefore, all listed statements are correct.

answer.text: It cannot be treated with iron supplements

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MOLECULAR_BASIS_OF_INHERITANCE_MCQ_Q08 - Biological roles and properties of AUG codon

questiontext.text: Which of the following is true with respect to AUG?

generalfeedback.text:
Conceptual Principle
The genetic code is degenerate, non-overlapping, and near-universal, with specific triplets dedicated to translation initiation.

Evaluation of Concepts
The triplet codon AUG serves dual functions: it acts as the primary initiation (start) codon signalling the assembly of the translation complex, and it unambiguously codes exclusively for the amino acid methionine (formylmethionine in prokaryotes). Furthermore, because the genetic code is universal across biological domains, AUG specifies methionine in both prokaryotes and eukaryotes.

Final Conclusion
AUG codes for methionine only, functions as the initiation codon, and specifies methionine in both prokaryotes and eukaryotes; thus, all the stated properties are true.

answer.text: It codes for methionine in both prokaryotes and eukaryotes

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MOLECULAR_BASIS_OF_INHERITANCE_MCQ_Q09 - Evolutionary origin of the first genetic material

questiontext.text: The first genetic material could be:

generalfeedback.text:
Conceptual Principle
The 'RNA World' hypothesis posits that early prebiotic life relied on ribonucleic acid molecules to mediate both heredity and biochemical catalysis.

Evaluation of Concepts
Extensive biochemical evidence demonstrates that essential biological processes—including translation, protein synthesis, and splicing—evolved around RNA. RNA can act both as a carrier of genetic information and as an active biocatalyst (ribozyme). DNA subsequently evolved from RNA through chemical modifications (such as 2'-deoxygenation and thymine substitution) that conferred superior structural and chemical stability for long-term genome storage.

Final Conclusion
Ribonucleic acid (RNA) was the primordial genetic material.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MOLECULAR_BASIS_OF_INHERITANCE_MCQ_Q10 - Presence of exons and introns in mature eukaryotic mRNA

questiontext.text: With regard to mature mRNA in eukaryotes:

generalfeedback.text:
Conceptual Principle
Eukaryotic structural genes possess a split-gene arrangement where coding sequences are interrupted by non-coding intervening sequences.

Evaluation of Concepts
The initial primary transcript produced in eukaryotes is heterogeneous nuclear RNA (hnRNA), which contains alternating coding segments (exons) and non-coding segments (introns). During post-transcriptional processing in the nucleus, the spliceosome removes introns via splicing and ligates the exons together in the proper sequence to produce mature mRNA, which is subsequently transported to the cytoplasm for translation.

Final Conclusion
In mature eukaryotic mRNA, exons are preserved and expressed, whereas introns are spliced out and absent.

answer.text: exons and introns do not appear in the mature RNA
exons appear but introns do not appear in the mature RNA
introns appear but exons do not appear in the mature RNA
both exons and introns appear in the mature RNA

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MOLECULAR_BASIS_OF_INHERITANCE_MCQ_Q11 - Highest and lowest gene count human chromosomes

questiontext.text: The human chromosome with the highest and least number of genes in them are respectively:

generalfeedback.text:
Conceptual Principle
The Human Genome Project mapped and quantified the distribution of protein-coding genes across all human chromosomes.

Evaluation of Concepts
According to the definitive sequencing data generated by the Human Genome Project, human Chromosome 1 is the largest autosome and carries the greatest number of genes (approximately 2968 genes). In contrast, the human Y chromosome is a small sex chromosome with the fewest genes among all chromosomes (containing only 231 genes).

Final Conclusion
Chromosome 1 has the highest number of genes, while the Y chromosome has the fewest genes.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MOLECULAR_BASIS_OF_INHERITANCE_MCQ_Q12 - Scientific contributions to the DNA double helix model

questiontext.text: Who amongst the following scientists had no contribution in the development of the double helix model for the structure of DNA?

generalfeedback.text:
Conceptual Principle
Elucidation of the three-dimensional double helix structure of DNA combined physical crystallographic data with quantitative biochemical base-ratio principles.

Evaluation of Concepts
Watson and Crick formulated their iconic 1953 double helix model by integrating the X-ray crystallographic diffraction patterns produced by Rosalind Franklin and Maurice Wilkins with the base-pairing equimolar rules discovered by Erwin Chargaff. In contrast, Matthew Meselson and Franklin Stahl conducted their density-gradient centrifugation experiments in 1958 to prove the semi-conservative replication mechanism of DNA, years after the double helix structure had already been established.

Final Conclusion
Meselson and Stahl did not contribute to the initial structural development of the double helix model.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MOLECULAR_BASIS_OF_INHERITANCE_MCQ_Q13 - Nucleotide modification preventing polymerisation in DNA synthesis

questiontext.text: DNA is a polymer of nucleotides which are linked to each other by 3'-5' phosphodiester bond. To prevent polymerisation of nucleotides, which of the following modifications would you choose?

generalfeedback.text:
Conceptual Principle
Phosphodiester bond synthesis proceeds through a nucleophilic attack by the free 3'-hydroxyl group of the elongating strand on the \( \alpha \)-phosphate of an incoming nucleoside triphosphate.

Evaluation of Concepts
In DNA, deoxyribose already naturally lacks a hydroxyl group at the 2'-position (having only a hydrogen atom, -H); therefore, altering the 2'-position does not affect phosphodiester polymerisation. Polymerisation strictly requires the 3'-OH group of the existing nucleotide. If the 3'-OH group is removed or replaced with an unreactive group (as seen in dideoxynucleotides), no phosphodiester bond can be created with the next incoming deoxynucleotide, immediately arresting further chain extension.

Final Conclusion
Chain polymerisation is terminated by removing or replacing the 3'-OH group on the deoxyribose ring.

answer.text: Remove/Replace 2' OH group with some other group in deoxy ribose

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MOLECULAR_BASIS_OF_INHERITANCE_MCQ_Q14 - Mechanism causing discontinuous synthesis in DNA replication

questiontext.text: Discontinuous synthesis of DNA occurs in one strand, because:

generalfeedback.text:
Conceptual Principle
DNA replication forks expose two antiparallel template strands simultaneously, but DNA polymerase operates with strict unidirectional catalytic polarity.

Evaluation of Concepts
DNA-dependent DNA polymerase can catalyse the addition of nucleotides strictly in the 5' to 3' direction. Because the parental strands run antiparallel (one 3' to 5' and the other 5' to 3'), the template oriented 3' to 5' supports continuous synthesis moving into the replication fork. However, on the template oriented 5' to 3', synthesis must proceed in the 5' to 3' direction away from the progressing fork, generating short Okazaki fragments that are synthesised discontinuously.

Final Conclusion
Discontinuous synthesis occurs because DNA-dependent DNA polymerase catalyses nucleotide addition solely in the 5' to 3' direction.

answer.text: DNA molecule being synthesised is very long
DNA dependent DNA polymerase catalyses polymerisation only in one direction (5' → 3')
DNA ligase joins the short stretches of DNA

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MOLECULAR_BASIS_OF_INHERITANCE_MCQ_Q15 - Transcriptional stage catalysed by core RNA polymerase

questiontext.text: Which of the following steps in transcription is catalysed by RNA polymerase?

generalfeedback.text:
Conceptual Principle
Prokaryotic RNA polymerase core enzyme requires transient regulatory factors to initiate and terminate transcription accurately.

Evaluation of Concepts
The core RNA polymerase enzyme alone has intrinsic catalytic activity capable of polymerising ribonucleotides, which drives the elongation phase of transcription. To initiate transcription at specific promoter sites, the core enzyme must associate with the initiation factor (\( \sigma \) factor). To terminate transcription at terminator sequences, it requires association with the termination factor (\( \rho \) factor). Hence, the core RNA polymerase enzyme intrinsically catalyses only the elongation phase.

Final Conclusion
RNA polymerase inherently catalyses the elongation step of transcription.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MOLECULAR_BASIS_OF_INHERITANCE_MCQ_Q16 - Primary control level of prokaryotic gene expression

questiontext.text: Control of gene expression in prokaryotes take place at the level of:

generalfeedback.text:
Conceptual Principle
In prokaryotic cells, transcription and translation occur coupled in the same compartment due to the absence of a defined nuclear envelope.

Evaluation of Concepts
Because ribosomes can begin translating an mRNA transcript while it is still being synthesised by RNA polymerase, the primary and predominant checkpoint for controlling gene expression in prokaryotes occurs at the level of transcription initiation. Regulating the access and binding affinity of RNA polymerase to the promoter regulates whether the gene product will be produced.

Final Conclusion
Gene expression in prokaryotes is primarily regulated at the level of transcription.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MOLECULAR_BASIS_OF_INHERITANCE_MCQ_Q17 - Function of regulatory proteins in prokaryotic transcription

questiontext.text: Which of the following statements is correct about the role of regulatory proteins in transcription in prokaryotes?

generalfeedback.text:
Conceptual Principle
Prokaryotic operons and genes are governed by both positive and negative transcriptional regulatory mechanisms.

Evaluation of Concepts
Regulatory proteins bind to specific DNA sequences adjacent to promoters to modulate transcription. When a regulatory protein enhances RNA polymerase binding and upregulates transcription, it functions positively as an activator. When a regulatory protein blocks RNA polymerase access to the promoter and shuts down transcription, it functions negatively as a repressor. Therefore, prokaryotic regulatory proteins can act as both activators and repressors depending on the operon system.

Final Conclusion
Regulatory proteins in prokaryotes can function both as activators and as repressors.

answer.text: They interact with RNA polymerase but do not affect the expression
They can act both as activators and as repressors

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MOLECULAR_BASIS_OF_INHERITANCE_MCQ_Q18 - Last human chromosome sequenced in genome project

questiontext.text: Which was the last human chromosome to be completely sequenced:

generalfeedback.text:
Conceptual Principle
The Human Genome Project sequenced all 24 distinct human chromosomes, completing them sequentially according to physical size and structural complexity.

Evaluation of Concepts
Chromosome 1 is the largest human chromosome, containing the largest total base pair count and the greatest number of genes. Due to its enormous length and complexity, its sequencing required extensive time and effort. Its completed sequence was finalized and published in May 2006, making it the last of the human chromosomes to be completely sequenced.

Final Conclusion
Chromosome 1 was the final human chromosome to be completely sequenced.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MOLECULAR_BASIS_OF_INHERITANCE_MCQ_Q19 - Diverse biological functions of ribonucleic acid

questiontext.text: Which of the following are the functions of RNA?

generalfeedback.text:
Conceptual Principle
Ribonucleic acid functions in various specialized forms to execute gene expression and protein synthesis in living cells.

Evaluation of Concepts
Messenger RNA (mRNA) carries encoded genetic sequences transcribed from nuclear DNA to ribosomes for translation. Transfer RNA (tRNA) acts as an adapter molecule, binding specific amino acids and transferring them to matching codons on mRNA. Ribosomal RNA (rRNA) constitutes structural and catalytic components of ribosomes (including peptidyl transferase activity). Consequently, all of the described activities represent canonical functions of RNA.

Final Conclusion
RNA acts as an information messenger, an amino acid transporter, and a structural component of ribosomes; thus, all the listed roles are functions of RNA.

answer.text: It is a carrier of genetic information from DNA to ribosomes synthesising polypeptides.
It is a constituent component of ribosomes.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MOLECULAR_BASIS_OF_INHERITANCE_MCQ_Q20 - Determination of DNA strandedness using Chargaff rules

questiontext.text: While analysing the DNA of an organism a total number of 5386 nucleotides were found out of which the proportion of different bases were: Adenine = 29%, Guanine = 17%, Cytosine = 32%, Thymine = 17%. Considering the Chargaff's rule it can be concluded that:

generalfeedback.text:
Given Data and Conditions
Total nucleotide count: \( 5386\text{ nucleotides} \).
Base proportions: \( \text{Adenine (A)} = 29\% \), \( \text{Guanine (G)} = 17\% \), \( \text{Cytosine (C)} = 32\% \), \( \text{Thymine (T)} = 17\% \).

Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Chargaff's base-pairing rules state that in any double-stranded DNA molecule, purines pair complementarily with pyrimidines, resulting in equal molar ratios: \( [\text{A}] = [\text{T}] \) and \( [\text{G}] = [\text{C}] \).

Relevant Formulae and Principles
For double-stranded DNA: \( \frac{[\text{A}]}{[\text{T}]} = 1 \) and \( \frac{[\text{G}]}{[\text{C}]} = 1 \). Any significant deviation indicates that the nucleic acid is single-stranded.

Step-by-Step Working
Comparing the given proportions:
\( [\text{A}] = 29\% \neq [\text{T}] = 17\% \)
\( [\text{G}] = 17\% \neq [\text{C}] = 32\% \)
Because base-pairing equivalence is absent, the DNA molecule does not exist as a complementary double helix.

Check and Final Answer
The total percentage equals \( 29\% + 17\% + 32\% + 17\% = 95\% \) (within analytical rounding), and the lack of base equivalence confirms that the DNA is single-stranded (characteristic of bacteriophage \( \phi \times 174 \)).

answer.text: it is a double stranded circular DNA
It is a double stranded linear DNA

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MOLECULAR_BASIS_OF_INHERITANCE_MCQ_Q21 - Definition of complementary DNA synthesised from RNA

questiontext.text: In some viruses, DNA is synthesised by using RNA as template. Such a DNA is called:

generalfeedback.text:
Conceptual Principle
Certain RNA viruses (retroviruses) reverse the normal flow of genetic information by generating DNA copies from their RNA templates.

Evaluation of Concepts
The enzyme reverse transcriptase (an RNA-dependent DNA polymerase) catalyses the synthesis of a DNA strand complementary to an RNA template. The DNA produced from an RNA template via this reverse transcription process is referred to as complementary DNA (cDNA). In contrast, A-DNA and B-DNA represent structural helical conformations of double-stranded DNA, and rDNA denotes recombinant DNA or ribosomal DNA.

Final Conclusion
DNA synthesised from an RNA template is termed complementary DNA (cDNA).

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MOLECULAR_BASIS_OF_INHERITANCE_MCQ_Q22 - Isotope ratios in fourth generation Meselson-Stahl experiment

questiontext.text: If Meselson and Stahl's experiment is continued for four generations in bacteria, the ratio of \(^{15}\text{N}/^{15}\text{N} : ^{15}\text{N}/^{14}\text{N} : ^{14}\text{N}/^{14}\text{N}\) containing DNA in the fourth generation would be:

generalfeedback.text:
Given Data and Conditions
Initial state (Generation 0): Bacteria grown exclusively in \(^{15}\text{N}\), yielding \(1\) double-stranded DNA molecule where both strands contain \(^{15}\text{N}\) (heavy, \(^{15}\text{N}/^{15}\text{N}\)).
Subsequent growth: Bacteria are shifted to a medium containing exclusively \(^{14}\text{N}\) for four consecutive generations.

Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Replication is semi-conservative: each duplex unwinds and each parental strand serves as a template for synthesizing a new strand containing the ambient isotope (\(^{14}\text{N}\)).

Relevant Formulae and Principles
After \(n\) generations, the total number of duplex DNA molecules is \(2^n\).
The initial two parental \(^{15}\text{N}\) strands are conserved indefinitely and remain distributed among exactly two hybrid molecules (\(^{15}\text{N}/^{14}\text{N}\)). All other newly formed strands contain \(^{14}\text{N}\).

Step-by-Step Working
For generation \(n = 4\):
Total DNA molecules = \(2^4 = 16\).
Heavy molecules (\(^{15}\text{N}/^{15}\text{N}\)) = \(0\).
Hybrid molecules (\(^{15}\text{N}/^{14}\text{N}\)) = \(2\).
Light molecules (\(^{14}\text{N}/^{14}\text{N}\)) = \(16 - 2 = 14\).
The ratio of \(^{15}\text{N}/^{15}\text{N} : ^{15}\text{N}/^{14}\text{N} : ^{14}\text{N}/^{14}\text{N}\) is \(0 : 2 : 14\), which simplifies to \(0 : 1 : 7\).

Check and Final Answer
The sum of the simplified terms \(0 + 1 + 7 = 8\) matches half the total pool (\(16/2 = 8\)), confirming the simplified ratio \(0:1:7\).

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MOLECULAR_BASIS_OF_INHERITANCE_MCQ_Q23 - Deducing RNA transcript sequence from coding strand

questiontext.text:
If the sequence of nitrogen bases of the coding strand of DNA in a transcription unit is:

5' - A T G A A T G - 3',

the sequence of bases in its RNA transcript would be:

generalfeedback.text:
Conceptual Principle
During transcription, RNA polymerase synthesizes RNA complementary to the template strand; consequently, the RNA sequence is identical to the coding strand except for the substitution of uracil for thymine.

Evaluation of Concepts
The coding strand and the synthesized RNA transcript possess the exact same 5' to 3' polarity and base sequence, with the sole chemical difference that thymine (T) in DNA is replaced by uracil (U) in RNA. Given the coding strand sequence 5' - A T G A A T G - 3', replacing each thymine (T) directly with uracil (U) yields the RNA transcript sequence 5' - A U G A A U G - 3'.

Final Conclusion
The sequence of bases in the resulting RNA transcript is 5' - A U G A A U G - 3'.

answer.text: 5' - A U G A A U G - 3'
5' - U A C U U A C - 3'
5' - C A U U C A U - 3'
5' - G U A A G U A - 3'

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MOLECULAR_BASIS_OF_INHERITANCE_MCQ_Q24 - Transcription domain of RNA polymerase holoenzyme

questiontext.text: The RNA polymerase holoenzyme transcribes:

generalfeedback.text:
Conceptual Principle
Transcription units contain non-transcribed regulatory docking regions alongside transcribed genetic regions.

Evaluation of Concepts
The promoter functions as the specific binding and recognition sequence for the RNA polymerase holoenzyme (incorporating the sigma factor). Transcription initiation starts downstream of the promoter at the transcription start site (+1 site); therefore, the promoter itself is not transcribed. Polymerisation proceeds across the structural gene and through the terminator region, where RNA synthesis ceases and the transcript is released. Thus, the actual transcribed domain comprises the structural gene and the terminator region.

Final Conclusion
The RNA polymerase holoenzyme transcribes the structural gene and the terminator region.

answer.text: the promoter, structural gene and the terminator region
the structural gene and the terminator region

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MOLECULAR_BASIS_OF_INHERITANCE_MCQ_Q25 - Anticodon base sequence pairing with AUG codon

questiontext.text: If the base sequence of a codon in mRNA is 5'-AUG-3', the sequence of tRNA pairing with it must be:

generalfeedback.text:
Conceptual Principle
Codon-anticodon base pairing between mRNA and tRNA occurs through antiparallel, complementary hydrogen bonding.

Evaluation of Concepts
The mRNA codon is given as 5' - A - U - G - 3'.
Complementary base pairing assigns:
Adenine (A) pairs with Uracil (U),
Uracil (U) pairs with Adenine (A),
Guanine (G) pairs with Cytosine (C).
Because the strands align in an antiparallel orientation, the tRNA anticodon matches the codon as 3' - U - A - C - 5'. Written in standard biochemical direction from the 5' to 3' terminus, this anticodon sequence is 5' - C - A - U - 3'.

Final Conclusion
The sequence of the pairing tRNA anticodon in the 5' to 3' direction is 5' - CAU - 3'.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MOLECULAR_BASIS_OF_INHERITANCE_MCQ_Q26 - Amino acid attachment terminal on transfer RNA

questiontext.text: The amino acid attaches to the tRNA at its:

generalfeedback.text:
Conceptual Principle
Transfer RNA possesses distinct functional structural domains responsible for codon recognition and amino acid esterification.

Evaluation of Concepts
The cloverleaf secondary structure of tRNA folds into an L-shaped tertiary form. At the opposite end from the anticodon loop, the tRNA has an amino acid acceptor stem that terminates in an unpaired single-stranded 5'-CCA-3' sequence at its 3'-end. Aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase covalently links the carboxyl group of the cognate amino acid to the 3'-hydroxyl group (-OH) of the terminal adenosine nucleotide at this 3'-end.

Final Conclusion
The cognate amino acid attaches covalently to the 3'-end of the tRNA molecule.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MOLECULAR_BASIS_OF_INHERITANCE_MCQ_Q27 - Ribosomal subunit binding during translation initiation

questiontext.text: To initiate translation, the mRNA first binds to:

generalfeedback.text:
Conceptual Principle
Ribosomal translation begins with the sequential assembly of ribosomal subunits and initiation factors on the mRNA transcript.

Evaluation of Concepts
In translation initiation, free ribosomes exist dissociated as independent smaller and larger subunits. The process begins when the smaller ribosomal subunit (30S in prokaryotes or 40S in eukaryotes) binds specifically to the mRNA at the ribosome binding site near the 5'-end. Once the initiator tRNA pairs with the AUG start codon on the small subunit, the larger ribosomal subunit is recruited to assemble the functional initiation complex.

Final Conclusion
Translation initiates when mRNA first binds to the smaller ribosomal subunit.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MOLECULAR_BASIS_OF_INHERITANCE_MCQ_Q28 - Molecular mechanism switching on the lac operon

questiontext.text: In E. coli, the lac operon gets switched on when:

generalfeedback.text:
Conceptual Principle
The lactose (lac) operon of Escherichia coli is an inducible operon subject to negative transcriptional control by a repressor protein.

Evaluation of Concepts
Under default conditions, the repressor protein (synthesized by the regulator i-gene) binds tightly to the operator region, physically blocking RNA polymerase from transcribing the structural genes. When lactose is introduced, it is converted to allolactose, which acts as an inducer. Lactose/allolactose binds directly to the repressor protein, causing a conformational change that inactivates the repressor and prevents it from binding to the operator. This derepression allows RNA polymerase to proceed with transcription, switching the operon on.

Final Conclusion
The lac operon is switched on when lactose is present and binds to the repressor, inactivating it.

answer.text: lactose is present and it binds to the repressor
lactose is present and it binds to RNA polymerase

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MOLECULAR_BASIS_OF_INHERITANCE_MCQ_Q09 - Sedimentation profile of DNA ligase mutant replication

questiontext.text: Replication was allowed to take place in the presence of radioactive deoxynucleotides precursors in E. coli that was a mutant for DNA ligase. Newly synthesised radioactive DNA was purified and strands were separated by denaturation. These were centrifuged using density gradient centrifugation. Which of the following would be a correct result?

generalfeedback.text:
Given Data and Conditions
Replication is conducted in a mutant strain of Escherichia coli lacking functional DNA ligase.
Radioactive deoxynucleotide precursors are present during synthesis, incorporating radioactivity into nascent DNA.
Newly synthesized DNA is purified, denatured into single strands, and separated by density gradient centrifugation according to molecular weight.

Assumptions and Sign Conventions
DNA replication is semiconservative and semi-discontinuous.
High molecular weight corresponds to long, continuous polynucleotide strands.
Low molecular weight corresponds to short, unjoined Okazaki fragments.

Relevant Formulae and Principles
DNA-dependent DNA polymerase synthesizes DNA exclusively in the 5' to 3' direction.
The leading strand is synthesized continuously, producing full-length, high-molecular-weight DNA.
The lagging strand is synthesized discontinuously as short Okazaki fragments.
DNA ligase is specifically required to form phosphodiester bonds that link adjacent Okazaki fragments into an unbroken high-molecular-weight strand.

Step-by-Step Working
Continuous synthesis along the leading strand proceeds uninterrupted, incorporating radioactive precursors to form full-length, high-molecular-weight radioactive strands.
On the lagging strand, Okazaki fragments are synthesized with radioactive precursors; however, because the cell lacks functional DNA ligase, these fragments cannot be covalently joined together.
Upon denaturation into single strands, the high-molecular-weight leading strands separate from the low-molecular-weight Okazaki fragments.
Centrifugation in a density gradient separates these two size classes into two distinct zones: one representing high-molecular-weight continuous strands and the other representing low-molecular-weight unjoined fragments.

Check and Final Answer
Because one strand is continuous and the other remains entirely fragmented, radioactivity is distributed between two distinct molecular weight fractions. The correct sedimentation profile exhibits two distinct radioactivity peaks: one at high molecular weight and another at low molecular weight.
